questions.questionText: India’s BioE3 Policy (Biotechnology for Economy, Environment, and Employment) is a strategic step towards building a sustainable bioeconomy. Examine the key mechanisms through which the policy seeks to strengthen the biomanufacturing ecosystem.

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Introduce your answer by giving a brief background of the policy.
• In the body of your answer, examine important mechanisms intended to strengthen the biomanufacturing ecosystem.
• Conclude by highlighting the alignment of the policy with the broader national objectives. | | --- | In August 2024, the Union Cabinet approved India's BioE3 Policy (Biotechnology for Economy, Environment, and Employment) as a strategic initiative for fostering high performance (advanced) biomanufacturing. The policy envisages the following key mechanisms to strengthen the biomanufacturing ecosystem in the country: 1. a)Creation of Biomanufacturing Hubs and Biofoundries across India to facilitate the scaling up of production processes and efficient manufacture of bio-based products; b)co-locating these hubs with existing research and infrastructure centers to foster innovation and accelerate the translation and commercialization of biotechnological advancements. 2. a)Integration of AI technologies into biomanufacturing processes through the establishment of Bio-AI Hubs; b)these hubs serve as centers of excellence, fostering interdisciplinary collaboration among academia, industry, and research institutions; c) they enable acceleration of data analysis, optimize production processes, and enhance decision-making in areas such as genomics, proteomics, and synthetic biology. 3. a)Introduction of the Bio-RIDE framework, which integrates biotechnology research and entrepreneurship under a cohesive policy structure; b)development of a skilled workforce through developing specialised training programs and higher education programs/curricula, in collaboration with industry leaders. 4. a)Focus on six thematic sectors of national importance viz. (i) bio-based chemicals and enzymes, (ii)precision biotherapeutics, (iii)climate resilient agriculture, (iv)functional foods, (v) carbon capture and utilization, (vi)futuristic marine and space research); b) the policy aims at driving innovation and commercialization in these sectors, which are critical to India's economic and environmental goals. Overall, the BioE3 policy aligns with the goal of a ‘Net Zero’ economy by 2070 and the vision of the ‘LiFE mission.’ It is expected to steer India on the path of accelerated ‘Green Growth’ by promoting ‘Circular Bioeconomy’. The Policy will foster sustainability, innovation, and responsiveness to global challenges and lays down the Bio-vision for Viksit Bharat. (270 words) Additional reading: BioE3 Policy Initiative |ForumIAS Centre’s new BioE3 policy: How can biotechnology be harnessed for economic development? | Explained News - The Indian Express Extra marks/content differentiation: 1. Quotes: • “As biology meets technology, biotechnology emerges as the architect of groundbreaking scientific innovations: from cellular mastery to societal progress. • From the lab to the field, from cells to societies, biotechnology carves the path from scientific insight to revolutionary applications.” 2. International Best practices: The European Union Bioeconomy Strategy aims to boost innovation and support European companies in making a success of the green transition. The strategy is expected to make EU businesses more competitive and increase green jobs – without damaging nature. The main goals of the strategy are: • Ensuring the long-term competitiveness of the EU bioeconomy and investment security. Identifying measures to scale up and commercialise existing and emerging biotech solutions and bio-based products. • Increasing resource-efficient and circular use of biological resources. Transforming the use and valuation of biomass resources, prioritizing extended high-value applications while encouraging industries and consumers to embrace circular practices. • Securing the competitive and sustainable supply of biomass, both domestically and from outside the EU. Strengthening the role of primary producers, generating wealth in rural areas by creating jobs and diversifying incomes for foresters and farmers and rewarding them for the preservation of ecosystems. • Positioning the EU in the rapidly expanding international market for bio-based materials, biomanufacturing, biochemicals, and agri-food and biotech sectors. This will be done, in particular, by steering existing foreign policy mechanisms.

questions.microtag: Discuss, Dr. Verghese Kurien, India's dairy sector
questions.questionText: Discuss the role of Dr. Verghese Kurien in revolutionising India’s dairy sector and empowering rural communities.

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Introduce your answer by giving a brief description about Dr.
• Kurien’s legacy as the Father of India’s White Revolution.
• In the body, highlight the pivotal role played by him in revolutionizing India’s dairy sector and empowering rural communities.
• Conclude your answer by mentioning some of the accolades earned by him. | | --- | Dr. Verghese Kurien is considered the key architect behind India’s transformation from a milk-deficit nation into the world’s largest milk producer. He is popularly known as the Father of the White Revolution in India. The role of Dr. Verghese Kurien in revolutionising India’s dairy sector and empowering rural communities: 1. a) Played a pivotal role in transforming the Kaira District Cooperative Milk Producers’ Union Limited (KDCMPUL) into the successful enterprise known as Amul; b) infused technology in the supply chain (standard fat checking machine, pasteurization, powder production, cooling and packaging units); c)realised the importance of branding in dairy sector and came out with the name “Amul”(registered in 1957), which has served as a model for cooperatives in several parts of the world. 2. a)Championed and institutionalized the three tier structure- Village societies, District Union and State federations; b) established systems ensuring farmers received remunerative prices; c) as the founding chairman of the National Dairy Development Board(NDDB) led the replication of the “Anand model” nationwide. 3. a)Launched “Operation Flood” in 1970 under NDDB; b)catapulted India to self-sufficiency and the world’s top milk producer by 1998; c)milk output surged from ~23 MT (1968–69) to ~239 MT (2023-24),per‑capita consumption nearly quadrupled (124gm/day in 1950-51 to 471gm/day in 2023-24). 4. a)Founded Institute of Rural Management Anand(IRMA) in 1979 for cooperative management education and to train rural managers; b)initiated edible-oil cooperative (“Dhara” in 1979) and and the Mother Dairy fruit and vegetable project in Delhi (aimed to provide a direct link between fruit and vegetable growers and consumers). 5. a)Over 85,000 village dairy co-operatives formed inspired from Amul model, empowering 15 million farmers (FAO report on Dairy Development in India); b)promoted inclusion of women in dairy cooperatives, contributing to economic independence and social mobility(e.g.,Mahila Dairy Cooperative Societies). 6. a)Contributed to improved animal health through cooperative veterinary services; b) contributed significantly to improved nutrition in rural areas; c) pioneered a model of decentralised development through localising production, processing, and profits; d)strengthened social cohesion by breaking caste and religious distinctions. Dr.Kurien’s main contribution has been as an institution builder,empowering people to develop themselves as he believed that people are the greatest asset of a country. His contribution has earned him many accolades including Padma Vibhushan (1999) and ‘Ramon Magsaysay award (1963). (364 words) Additional reading: Indian agriculture needs a Verghese Kurien -ForumIAS Blog Verghese Kurien, the engineer who 'dairied' to dream and ushered in the White Revolution https://forumias.com/blog/tribhuvandas-patel/ Extra marks/content differentiation: 1. Quote: • “Milk is the only commodity which has to be collected twice a day, every day of the year. Thus, cooperatives are the only logical system for the dairy industry. About 85% of the industry in the US, Denmark and Australia is run by cooperatives. No other system will work for milk.”- Dr. Verghese Kurien • “Dr Kurien's greatest contribution was to give a position of pre-eminence to the farmer".- former PM Dr. Manohan Singh 2. Government initiatives: • The Ministry of Cooperation has launched cooperative-led "White Revolution 2.0” aimed at expanding cooperative coverage, employment generation and women's empowerment. • Its objective is to “increase the milk procurement from dairy cooperatives by 50% from the present level over next five years by providing market access to dairy farmers in uncovered areas and increasing the share of dairy cooperatives in the organised sector. • For the above purpose, the Ministry of Cooperation has envisaged to set up 75,000 new Dairy Cooperative Societies (DCSs) in uncovered panchayats/villages and strengthen 46,422 existing DCSs. • These DCSs will be provided market linkage either by expanding the existing milk routes or by creating new milk routes. NDDB will coordinate various activities related to White Revolution 2.0. • Women play an indispensable role in India’s dairy sector performing important work related to milking, feeding, managing cattle and ensuring animal health. • Nearly 70% of the workforce in dairy farming consists of women, yet their contribution often remains undervalued due to the unorganized nature of the sector. Women led dairy cooperatives have emerged as powerful tools for their empowerment.

questions.questionText: What is gene therapy? What makes it a better treatment option than the conventional approaches?

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Introduce the answer by giving a brief explanation about gene therapy.
• In the body, discuss its advantages over conventional approaches.
• Next, mention the associated concerns and challenges.
• Conclude by emphasizing the need for adherence to regulatory framework. | | --- | According to the ICMR, Gene Therapy refers to the process of introduction, removal or change in content of an individual’s genetic material to treat a disease and achieve long term cure. It can work by following mechanisms: 1. Replacing a disease-causing gene with a healthy copy of the gene. 2. Inactivating a disease-causing gene that is not functioning properly. 3. Introducing a new or modified gene into the body to help treat a disease. Advantages of gene therapy over other conventional treatments are as follows: 1. a) Ability to address the root cause of the disease (repairing faulty genes). Conventional approaches usually offer only symptomatic treatment; b) greater promise to cure genetic disorders and rare diseases (e.g. OTOF gene therapy for restoring hearing loss). 2. a) Long-lasting benefits, offered by modified genes (e.g. CAR-T Cell therapy uses the body's own immune system to fight cancerous cells). Conventional approaches, however, need regular administration (e.g. insulin injections); b) lesser chances of disease relapse as compared to conventional approaches (e.g. cancer recurrence after chemotherapy). 3. a) Improved treatment efficiency (can be targeted to specific cells- e.g. CRISPR CaS 9); b) reduced risk of harmful side effects (e.g. hair loss after radiotherapy); c) ease of delivery of treatments (e.g. through injections). This can help avoid the complex conventional approaches (e.g. invasive surgeries for brain tumours). However, it also poses the following risks/challenges: 1. a) Immunological barriers (e.g. rejection of ‘foreign genes’); b) risk of unintended mutations (e.g. off target events in CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing) that can pose long-term side effects; c) ineffectiveness for complex, multifactorial diseases where the underlying genetic cause is unknown (e.g. Alzheimer's). 2. a) Likely to deepen existing health care divide (prohibitive costs, pharmaceutical monopolies); b) concerns due to technological development outpacing regulatory oversight; c) ethical considerations arising from artificial genetic selection and human intervention in “godly affairs” (e.g. germline editing to produce designer babies by Chinese biophysicist He Jiankui). India’s first home-grown gene therapy for cancer was launched at IIT Bombay (April 2024), marking a significant breakthrough in treating complex diseases like cancer. However, continuous advancements under a robust regulatory framework (ICMR's 2019 guidelines), while driving affordability (cell and gene therapy mission mooted by the Principal Scientific Advisor), are essential to address the associated concerns. (382 words) Additional reading: Explained: What is gene therapy? How is DNA used to treat genetic disorders? - Times of India Extra marks/content differentiation: 1. Quotes: • “The advance of genetic engineering makes it quite conceivable that we will begin to design our own evolutionary progress.” — Isaac Asimov • “I think the ethics and morals of genetic engineering are very complicated. It intrigues me.” — Roger Spottiswoode 2. Case study: Scientists from the CSIR-Institute of Genomics and Integrative Biology, New Delhi, have developed an enhanced genome-editing system that can modify DNA more precisely and more efficiently than existing CRISPR-based technologies. To enhance it without compromising its specificity, researchers led by Debojyoti Chakraborty and Souvik Maiti at CSIR-IGIB modified and engineered new versions of FnCas9. The researchers tinkered with amino acids in FnCas9 that recognise and interact with the PAM sequence on the host genome. By doing this, we increase the binding affinity of the Cas protein with the PAM sequence. The Cas9 can then sit on the DNA in a stronger configuration, and your gene editing becomes much more effective.The researchers also engineered the enhanced FnCas9 to be more flexible and edit regions of the genome that are otherwise harder to access.Experiments to measure enzyme activity showed that enhanced FnCas9 cut target DNA at a higher rate compared to unmodified FnCas9.
